name: Liberation theology
info: Liberation theology is a Christian theological approach that emphasises the liberation of the oppressed. It began among Latin American Catholic theologians in the 1960s, spread to other regions and traditions, and remains a subject of debate.

facts.where: Latin America, above all within the Catholic Church in Peru, Brazil, El Salvador and Uruguay; related theologies in the United States, South Africa, among Palestinians, India, South Korea and Ireland
facts.period: discussed in Latin America in the 1960s after the Second Vatican Council; term coined in 1971; Protestant calls for integral mission in the 1970s; height in the 1970s and 1980s; Vatican admonition in the mid-1980s; continuing influence since
facts.figures: Gustavo Gutiérrez, who coined the term; Leonardo Boff; Jon Sobrino; Juan Luis Segundo; Frei Betto; Óscar Romero; Hélder Câmara, Brazilian archbishop; Protestant advocates Rubem Alves, José Míguez Bonino and C. René Padilla
facts.outcome: grassroots ecclesial communities that mobilised for land reform, labour rights and democratic governance; criticism from Pope John Paul II and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith; waning prominence after the 1980s, with continuing influence in theology, scholarship and social movements

t: Liberation theology interprets the Gospel through the lens of the oppressed, and its best-known phrase, the preferential option for the poor, describes an obligation of those who call themselves Christian first of all to care for the poor and vulnerable.

It drew heavily on Marxist social analysis, though it did not adopt Marxism wholesale, and the Vatican's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, led by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, criticised it in the mid-1980s for excessive politicisation.

Its ideas spread beyond Latin America and beyond Catholicism, into black theology, Dalit theology, Palestinian liberation theology and Protestant thought, and Pope Francis later drew on liberationist ideas.
dyk: Hélder Câmara, the Brazilian archbishop, said: "When I give food to the poor, they call me a saint. When I ask why they are poor, they call me a communist."
ev: Liberation theologies are first discussed in Latin America, especially within Catholicism after the Second Vatican Council
Protestant advocates including C. René Padilla call for integral mission, emphasising evangelism and social responsibility
The Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez coins the term and writes A Theology of Liberation
Dalit theology emerges among the Dalit castes of the Indian subcontinent
The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith admonishes certain forms of Latin American liberation theology for their reliance on Marxism

sections.background:
Liberation theology developed within the Catholic Church in Latin America in the 1960s as a reaction to the poverty and social injustice of the region, which CEPAL deemed the most unequal in the world. Liberation theologies were first discussed in the Latin American context, especially within Catholicism, after the Second Vatican Council.

Its roots can be traced to precursors such as Catholic Action and to the influence of the Second Vatican Council, which inspired new approaches to addressing systemic poverty and inequality in Latin America. Its theological framework centres on interpreting the Gospel through the lens of the oppressed, and it also drew from broader socialist and anti-imperialist movements.

Canon law supplied one of its stated foundations: "The Christian faithful are also obliged to promote social justice and, mindful of the precept of the Lord, to assist the poor." More or less at the same time as the first publications of Latin American liberation theology, voices of black liberation theology and Womanist theology were also heard, so that several theologies of liberation arose in the same years.
sections.aims:
The central idea of the movement is the option for the poor, a phrase popularised by Frei Betto, Gustavo Gutiérrez, Leonardo Boff and the Jesuits Juan Luis Segundo and Jon Sobrino. In the form it takes in canon law, it indicates an obligation, on the part of those who would call themselves Christian, first and foremost to care for the poor and vulnerable.

Liberation theology often engages in socio-economic analysis and emphasises social concern for those marginalised because of their social class, race, ethnicity, gender and similar grounds. Its theoretical foundations draw heavily from Marxist social analysis, particularly its critique of structural inequality and class oppression. It does not adopt Marxism wholesale, but its use of concepts such as class struggle and its critique of global capitalism led to significant controversy within the Church.

In practice it was a driving force in the rise of grassroots ecclesial communities, in Spanish comunidades eclesiales de base. These communities mobilised marginalised populations to advocate for land reform, labour rights and democratic governance, and often served as spaces for political consciousness-raising, blending religious practices with calls for systemic change.
sections.events:
The term "liberation theology" was coined in 1971 by the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez, who wrote one of the movement's defining books, A Theology of Liberation. Latin America also produced Protestant advocates, among them Rubem Alves, José Míguez Bonino and C. René Padilla, who in the 1970s called for integral mission, emphasising evangelism and social responsibility.

The movement reached its height in the 1970s and 1980s. In El Salvador, figures such as Archbishop Óscar Romero became symbols of resistance against military regimes and human rights abuses. During the military dictatorship in Brazil, the archbishop Hélder Câmara called on clergy to engage in the struggle for justice without fear of identification with the revolutionary left, and refused to condemn armed resistance. In an interview with the Italian journalist Oriana Fallaci he said that it was not his choice, "not my road, not my way to apply the Gospels", but that he would never say "to use weapons against an oppressor is immoral or anti-Christian".

In the mid-1980s the Vatican's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF) issued an admonition because of the movement's reliance on "Marxism". Latin American liberation theology also influenced parts of the evangelical movement and Catholic bishops in the United States.
sections.people:
The Peruvian Gustavo Gutiérrez coined the term and wrote A Theology of Liberation. Other exponents include Leonardo Boff of Brazil, Jon Sobrino of El Salvador and Juan Luis Segundo of Uruguay, and Frei Betto helped to popularise the phrase "preferential option for the poor". Archbishop Óscar Romero became a symbol of resistance in El Salvador, and the archbishop Hélder Câmara a voice for engagement in the struggle for justice under military regimes.

Protestant advocates included Rubem Alves, José Míguez Bonino and C. René Padilla. Outside Latin America, James Hal Cone was one of the original advocates of black theology, which he described as "a rational study of the being of God in the world in light of the existential situation of an oppressed community, relating the forces of liberation to the essence of the Gospel, which is Jesus Christ". The writings of Allan Boesak and Desmond Tutu show how liberationist ideas shaped anti-apartheid activism in South Africa.

In Palestinian liberation theology, the Anglican cleric Naim Ateek founded the Sabeel Ecumenical Liberation Theology Center in Jerusalem, and the Catholic priest Rafiq Khoury wrote mostly in Arabic. In Belfast, the priest Des Wilson defended the right of communities failed by the state and the churches to create alternative institutions. Ali Shari'ati in Iran adapted liberationist principles to critique Western imperialism within a Shi'a framework.
sections.outcomes:
Liberation theology generated grassroots ecclesial communities that mobilised marginalised populations and influenced political and social movements across Latin America. It has been particularly influential in countries such as El Salvador. Its prominence has waned since its height in the 1970s and 1980s.

It also faced significant criticism. Pope John Paul II and the CDF, led by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, who later became Pope Benedict XVI, criticised it for what they perceived as excessive politicisation and alignment with communist ideologies. Ratzinger stated that "in itself, the expression 'theology of liberation' is a thoroughly valid term", but rejected certain forms of Latin American liberation theology for focusing on institutionalised or systemic sin and for identifying the Catholic Church hierarchy in South America as members of the same privileged class that had long been oppressing Indigenous populations from the arrival of Pizarro onward.

Some within the Catholic Church questioned its alignment with Marxist ideologies, particularly its use of class analysis and its perceived politicisation of theology. Others argued that its political activism blurred the boundaries between religion and politics, raising concerns about the church's role in revolutionary movements.
sections.legacy:
Theologies of liberation have developed in other parts of the world: black theology in the United States and South Africa, Palestinian liberation theology, Dalit theology in India, Minjung theology in South Korea, liberation theology in Ireland, Deaf liberation theology and a Christian peace movement associated with liberation theology. Dalit theology emerged in the 1980s, two decades after its Latin American counterpart, shares a number of its themes, and sees hope in the "Nazareth Manifesto" of Luke 4.

Liberation theology continues to influence contemporary theological and social movements. In the context of globalisation, its critique of neoliberal policies and its emphasis on solidarity among oppressed groups remain relevant. Pope Francis, the first Latin American pope, drew from liberationist ideas, particularly in his advocacy for economic justice and environmental stewardship, as seen in his encyclical Laudato Si'. This development signalled a renewed engagement with the movement's principles within the institutional Church.

Its legacy also includes its impact on academic discourse, where it has fostered interdisciplinary approaches to theology, sociology and political science. Scholars have analysed its role in decolonising knowledge and creating counter-hegemonic narratives, particularly within the Global South.

summary: Liberation theology is a Christian approach, begun among Latin American Catholic theologians in the 1960s, that reads the Gospel through the experience of the oppressed and urges an option for the poor. The Vatican criticised its use of Marxist analysis, yet it spread across regions and traditions and still shapes theology and social movements.
references: Gustavo Gutiérrez, A Theology of Liberation: History, Politics and Salvation (Orbis Books, 1988)
Christian Smith, The Emergence of Liberation Theology: Radical Religion and the Social Movement Theory (University of Chicago Press, 1991)
